title: Human approval checkpoints in Claude Code and the Agent SDK
titleVi: Các điểm phê duyệt của con người trong Claude Code và Agent SDK

units.text: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
What you will be able to do
Choose a Claude Code permission mode by how much of Claude's work a person must approve
Name the checkpoints that still reach a human in every permission mode
Trace a tool call through hooks, deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules and canUseTool, and predict which step decides it
Implement a canUseTool callback that sends a person's approval, changes or refusal back to Claude
Key concept
Human approval checkpoint
A point in the permission pipeline where a tool call stops until a person approves it, changes it or refuses it. The checkpoint only exists if no earlier step has already approved or denied the call.
In this lesson
Why an agent needs human approval checkpoints
Permission modes: how much the human reviews
Where the human sits in the permission order
canUseTool: routing tool calls to a person
Why an agent needs human approval checkpoints

An agent that can run shell commands, edit files or call external services will sometimes do something its user never meant. Anthropic's incident log lists real cases: deleting remote git branches after misreading an instruction, uploading an engineer's GitHub auth token to a compute cluster, and attempting migrations against a production database. None of these came from hostile intent. In each case the model was overeager and
takes initiative beyond what the user would approve

Human-in-the-loop validation means putting a person between the agent and those actions. The design problem is placing the person well. If every action asks for approval, people stop reading the prompts: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts. If nothing asks, nobody catches the deleted branch. A good design sends routine reads and edits through without a prompt and saves the person's attention for actions that are irreversible, touch shared infrastructure or send data outside the organisation.
Claude offers three surfaces for this. Claude Code uses
permission modes
. The Agent SDK uses a
canUseTool
callback that your application answers. Managed Agents use
permission policies
that pause a session until your client confirms. All three answer the same question: which calls run on their own and which ones wait for a person?
Checkpoint 1 of 8
Check yourself

A team sets up its coding agent so that every tool call waits for a person to approve it, including file reads and routine edits. They expect this to give the strongest protection against incidents such as a deleted remote branch. What does the lesson say will happen, and what is the better design?

Reviewers soon approve prompts without reading them. A better design lets routine reads and edits run on their own and asks a person only about irreversible actions, actions on shared infrastructure, or actions that send data outside the organisation.
The design is as safe as it gets. More prompts always mean more overeager actions get caught, so every call should ask for approval.
The design is too slow. A better approach removes every prompt and has a person review the agent's logs after the task, which catches the same mistakes.
The prompts are mostly wasted. The incidents come from hostile intent or prompt injection, so an agent trying to help needs no approval checkpoints.
Sources
Permission modes: how much the human reviews
A permission mode sets the baseline for how much a person reviews. In Claude Code you switch modes with Shift+Tab in the CLI, and in the SDK you set
. Going from
to
, each mode takes more decisions away from the person.
What each Claude Code permission mode runs without asking, and when to use it
Mode
What runs without asking
Best for
default
Reads only
Reviewing every action yourself, sensitive work
acceptEdits
Reads, file edits, and common filesystem commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp, etc.)
Iterating on code you're reviewing
plan
Reads, plus classifier-approved commands when auto mode is available
Exploring a codebase before changing it
auto
Everything, with background safety checks
Long tasks, reducing prompt fatigue
dontAsk
File reads inside your working directories and pre-approved tools; anything that would prompt is denied
Locked-down CI and scripts
bypassPermissions
Everything
Isolated containers and VMs only
Two modes give different kinds of human-in-the-loop control, and they are easy to confuse.
lets Claude investigate freely but keeps your source files untouched until a person signs off. Claude Code blocks edits until you approve a plan.
is for runs with no person present. It turns every would-be prompt into a denial, so a CI job never sits waiting on a question nobody will answer. Calls approved by
or allow rules still run. In the SDK,
is never called in this mode. A headless run with
behaves the same way: the few calls that would still prompt are denied instead.
In

mode a model-based classifier takes the human approver's place. Before shell commands and network requests run, it checks that they match what the user asked for. Approval fatigue is the reason it exists. It does not remove the person entirely.
Some actions reach a person in every mode, including
and
, which skips permission prompts except for the actions no mode auto-approves. These are:
tools matched by an explicit ask rule
connector tools your organisation set to ask, in sessions where that setting reaches Claude Code
tools that need user interaction: the built-in AskUserQuestion tool and MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction
rm and rmdir removals targeting a critical path
the cross-session messaging safeguards
Ask rules sit on that list. In brief, an ask rule names a tool or command pattern that always prompts (see
Permission rules: allow, ask and deny
). That makes an ask rule a checkpoint that survives a mode change. What the person sends back matters too. On a prompt they can attach a comment. If they choose
Yes
, Claude Code runs the action and then gives Claude the comment. If they choose
No
, the comment goes to Claude as the reason for the denial and Claude keeps working. A
No
without a comment on a main-conversation prompt stops the turn.
On the exam
Organisations can take the loosest modes away from users. In managed settings, set
to "disable" to block bypassPermissions, and set
to "disable" to remove auto mode.
Exam trap
In dontAsk mode, calls that are not pre-approved are routed to canUseTool or held until someone answers.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 2 of 8
Match them up
Match each permission mode to how it handles human review.
Tap a term, then the definition that fits it.
plan
acceptEdits
auto
dontAsk
bypassPermissions
Claude can explore the codebase freely, but source files stay untouched until a person approves the plan.
Pre-approved tools run, and every call that would prompt is denied at once, so an unattended CI job never waits for an answer.
A background classifier checks shell commands and network requests against what the user asked for, in place of routine prompts.
Skips prompts except for the actions no mode auto-approves. Use it only in isolated containers and VMs.
File edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir or mv run without a prompt, while other actions still ask.
Checkpoint 3 of 8
Check yourself
Developers often switch Claude Code to auto or bypassPermissions with Shift+Tab. The security lead wants a person to review every
whatever mode is active. Which configuration does that?
Have developers run in dontAsk mode, because dontAsk holds each push until a person answers.
Add an ask rule for Bash(git push *), because ask rules still prompt in auto and bypassPermissions modes.
Add a deny rule for Bash(git push *), because a deny rule sends the call to a person for review.
Set disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable" in managed settings, because blocking bypassPermissions alone means every push reaches a person.
Checkpoint 4 of 8
Exam question

A DevOps team runs a Claude agent unattended inside a CI pipeline to triage failing builds. No human is available to respond to interactive approval prompts during the run, so any tool call that isn't already pre-approved must be denied outright rather than left waiting on a prompt. Which permission mode configuration achieves this?
Set permissionMode to "dontAsk" and list the CI-safe tools in allowedTools, so listed calls run automatically and everything else is denied without ever reaching canUseTool.
Set permissionMode to "default" and omit a canUseTool callback entirely, so unmatched tool calls silently resolve to a denial once the SDK detects no callback is registered to answer them.

Set permissionMode to "acceptEdits" and rely on its file-edit auto-approval to cover the pipeline's needs, since filesystem and shell write operations outside that scope are denied automatically rather than queued for a prompt.
Set permissionMode to "plan" so Claude only proposes fixes without executing any tool, which removes the need for approval prompts because no tool calls are dispatched during the run.
Sources
Where the human sits in the permission order
In the Agent SDK, every tool call passes through a fixed sequence of steps. The first step that reaches a decision settles the call, and later steps never see it. The person, through
, is the last step. So whether a human ever sees a call depends on what every step before it did.
Agent SDK permission evaluation order, first step to last
Step
What it does to a call
1. Hooks
Custom code that can allow, deny, or modify the tool request
2. Deny rules
Block matching calls; nothing later can lift the block
3. Ask rules
Send matching calls for confirmation
4. Permission mode
bypassPermissions approves what reaches it; acceptEdits approves file operations; plan sends file-edit and shell-write tools to canUseTool; other modes fall through
5. Allow rules
A bare allowedTools entry such as "Read" approves the whole tool
6. canUseTool callback
Asks a person at runtime when no earlier step resolved the call
Predict first
A session runs in plan mode, and allowedTools includes an Edit rule. Claude proposes an edit to a source file. What happens to that call?
It is denied outright, because plan mode never executes edits
The allow rule approves it, because allow rules are explicit configuration
It goes to the canUseTool callback for a person to review
The order explains which configurations keep a person in the loop:
Plan mode keeps a reviewer on every write.

The mode step comes before allow rules, so in plan mode no write can be auto-approved. A lead who wants to see each diff before it lands can let Claude investigate with read-only tools while every proposed edit goes to the callback. acceptEdits does the opposite: edits land first and get reviewed afterwards.
A bare allow entry silences the callback.
An
entry such as
approves the whole tool before the callback is consulted. If you allow a tool and expect
to intercept it, the callback will never run for that tool.
A deny rule cannot be reversed from the callback.
Deny rules are step two. A call they block never reaches step six, so
cannot lift the block for a single call.
bypassPermissions only approves what reaches step four.
It approves everything that arrives at the mode step, so a hook or ask rule that already decided the call is not affected.
That last point is why a hook is the strongest checkpoint for a high-impact tool. Hooks run custom code on every matching call (see
Hooks: actions that always run

). A PreToolUse hook scoped to a wire-transfer tool decides at step one, before any rule or mode. It adds a second approval layer on top of the permission settings. If someone later switches the session to bypassPermissions, the hook's demand for human approval still holds, because the bypass step comes after it.
A CI job sets permissionMode to dontAsk and lists Bash(npm test) and Read in allowedTools. Claude tries to run git push. Who decides, and what is the outcome?
Exam traps
Switching a session to bypassPermissions overrides every approval checkpoint, including hooks and ask rules.
Why is that wrong?
Adding a tool to allowedTools still lets canUseTool inspect each call to it.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 5 of 8
Check yourself

An SDK application wants a person to approve each shell command, but it also wants Bash to work without friction. So it sets allowedTools to ["Read", "Bash"] and adds a canUseTool callback that shows each Bash command to an operator. During testing, Bash commands run and the operator never sees one. What explains this, and what fixes it?
The default permission mode approves shell commands before allow rules are checked. Switch to bypassPermissions so that every call is passed on to canUseTool.
canUseTool runs before allow rules but skips tools that are listed in allowedTools. Move Bash into an ask rule inside the callback itself.
canUseTool runs only after a deny rule blocks a call. Add a deny rule for Bash so that each command goes to the operator, who can then lift the block.
The bare "Bash" entry approves every Bash call at the allow-rule step, which comes before canUseTool. Remove Bash from allowedTools so its calls fall through to the callback.
Checkpoint 6 of 8
Exam question

A fintech company's Claude-powered agent can initiate wire transfers through a custom MCP tool. Even though the operations team has configured allowedTools to auto-approve most read and reporting tools, they want every wire-transfer tool call to require a human's explicit approval no matter what permission mode the session is later switched to, including bypassPermissions. Which approach best satisfies this requirement?

Register a PreToolUse hook scoped to the wire-transfer tool that returns permissionDecision "ask" for every call, since hooks execute before deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode check, and allow rules, and their decision holds even under bypassPermissions.

Add a bare allowedTools entry for the wire-transfer tool so it auto-approves, then depend on the canUseTool callback to intercept it, since bare allow rules approve every matching call before canUseTool is ever consulted, so the callback never runs for that tool.

Switch the session's permission mode to acceptEdits, expecting the wire-transfer tool to fall outside its file-edit scope and always route to canUseTool, though other tools under acceptEdits still fall through to any allow rules that already approve them.

Add the wire-transfer tool to disallowed_tools with a wildcard pattern so it is blocked by default, then have the canUseTool callback lift the deny rule per call, though deny rules are evaluated before canUseTool runs and cannot be reversed from inside that callback.
Checkpoint 7 of 8
Exam question

An engineering lead is building an agent with the Claude Agent SDK to investigate a suspected security vulnerability across a large codebase. She insists that no file be modified until she has personally reviewed and approved the exact edit Claude intends to make, through an approval callback in her own application. Which configuration best matches this workflow?

Run the session with permissionMode "plan" so Claude investigates with read-only tools, while every file-edit or shell-write call is routed to the canUseTool callback for her review, even when an allow rule matches.

Run the session with permissionMode "acceptEdits" so Claude edits files immediately as it investigates, then have her review the accumulated diff afterward before the branch is merged into the codebase.

Run the session with permissionMode "default" and add every source file path to disallowed_tools so Write and Edit calls against them are blocked, then remove each path from the deny list once she approves that specific change.
Run the session with permissionMode "bypassPermissions" and add an explicit ask rule for the Edit and Write tools, since ask rules are the only rule type evaluated before the bypass step is reached.
Sources
canUseTool: routing tool calls to a person

is how an Agent SDK application asks a person. The SDK calls it in two situations. The first is when Claude wants a tool that no permission rule or mode has auto-approved. The second is when Claude calls

to ask a clarifying question. The callback receives the tool name, the tool's input and a context object. You show those to a person, wait for their decision and return it. For Bash, the input carries
and
. For Write, it carries
and
. Those are the details a reviewer needs to see.
A minimal Python callback: ask the user, then return allow or deny
python

The callback returns one of two results, and each one sends something back to Claude. An allow result carries the input the tool will run with. That can be Claude's original input or a version the person edited. A deny result carries a message. The tool does not run, and Claude reads the message and continues.
The two canUseTool responses in each SDK language
Response
Python
TypeScript
Allow
PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=...)
{ behavior: "allow", updatedInput }
Deny
PermissionResultDeny(message=...)
{ behavior: "deny", message }
Those two shapes support six reviewer actions:
Approve: let the tool run as Claude requested.
Approve with changes: edit the input before execution, for example to sanitise a path or add a constraint.
Approve and remember: send back a rule from the context's
so matching calls skip the prompt next time.
Reject: block the tool and tell Claude why.
Suggest an alternative: block the call but point Claude towards what the user wants instead.
Redirect entirely: use streaming input to send Claude a completely new instruction.
Two wiring details catch people out. If you pass a
array, include
in it, or Claude's clarifying questions never reach the callback. In Python, the documented example also registers a dummy PreToolUse hook that returns
, because that workaround keeps the stream open for
. In TypeScript, the context argument also carries an
, which lets you cancel a prompt nobody is answering.
Apply it to your own work
Pick one tool your agent uses. When a reviewer refuses that call, what deny message would help Claude choose a better next step instead of retrying the same call?
